Aggregate demand is the total demand for all goods and services in an economy at a given average price level and in a given time period.
The total output of goods and services that firms in an economy are willing and able to supply at each price level in a given period.
The total output that firms in an economy are willing and able to produce at each price level.
Resources are allocated to produce the optimal mix of goods and services that meet the wants and needs of society, maximising society's welfare.
The firm is not producing at the point where P = MC, so there is underproduction and a deadweight welfare loss to society.
Acting against pure self-interest for moral or social reasons.

The idea that individuals may be influenced by the first piece of information they receive when making a decision, even if it is not relevant or accurate. e.g. a consumer may see a £100 product discounted to £80 and perceive it as a good deal, without checking the price at other stores.
A rise in the value of a currency against another.
When one party in a transaction has more or better information than the other, distorting the market outcome.

Non-discretionary changes in government spending and taxation that occur automatically in response to changes in economic activity, helping to stabilise the economic cycle without the government intervening.

The idea that individuals may be influenced by information that is readily available to them, rather than seeking out all the relevant information. e.g. deciding not to fly due to a recent plane crash, even though the risk of flying is statistically very low.
The mean output produced per unit of a variable factor, typically labour.
TR/Q. This is the price per unit and also the firm's demand curve.

Growth by merging with or taking over a supplier earlier in the supply chain. This can secure inputs and improve control over cost and quality. For example, if a car manufacturer merges with a tyre manufacturer, it is backward integrated.
A record of all financial transactions between one country and the rest of the world over a period, made up of the current account, the capital account and the financial account.
A statement of a bank's assets and liabilities at a particular point in time.
The interest rate the Bank of England pays commercial banks on the money they keep with it overnight. It is also called the base rate or the official interest rate.
Obstacles that make it difficult for new firms to enter a market, such as high sunk costs, patents, brand loyalty or control of a key input. They allow existing firms to sustain supernormal profit.
The reference year against which all other years are compared. The value of the variable in the base year is set to 100, and every other year is expressed relative to it.

The assumption that individuals are not always rational decision makers and that their decisions may be influenced by a range of psychological and social factors, which may lead to them making decisions that do not maximise their utility.
Anything that makes research results lean one way, so they no longer give a true picture of the market. It can creep in at several points:
A deal between two countries to reduce barriers to trade between them.

A tradable debt security issued by a government or a firm in order to borrow money. The buyer lends the issuer a sum of money and, in return, receives a fixed interest payment each year plus repayment of the original sum on a set date in the future.
A period when real GDP grows faster than its trend rate and the economy is working at or near full capacity.
Decisions are made with limited information, time, and cognitive ability.
The idea that individuals may not always act in their own best interests due to a lack of self control.
A name, logo or design that identifies a firm's products and sets them apart from rivals'.
The level of output at which total revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. At that output, total fixed costs + total variable costs = total sales revenue.
G > T. This means government spending is greater than tax revenue, so the government must borrow and national debt rises.
T > G. This means tax revenue is greater than government spending, so the surplus can be used to repay debt.
The moral principles that guide a firm's decisions, about what is right as well as what is legal or profitable.
A target a business sets itself, which guides its decisions and gives it a way to judge how well it is doing.
The most a firm can produce in a given period with its existing premises, machinery and staff.
The firm's current output as a percentage of its maximum possible output: CU (%) = Current outputMaximum output x 100
Records relatively minor capital transfers, such as debt forgiveness.
Long-term investment in infrastructure and assets such as roads, hospitals, and schools.
Refers to the rapid outflow of financial assets and capital from a country due to economic or political instability.
Goods bought by firms to produce other goods and services, such as machinery, tools and factories, rather than to satisfy consumer wants directly.
The removal of controls on moving money into and out of a country, so that firms and investors can invest abroad freely.
The ratio of a bank's capital - shareholders' funds and retained profit - to its risk-weighted assets.
Production that uses a high proportion of machinery and equipment compared with labour.
An economic system based on private ownership of the factors of production with the aim of generating profit.
A group of firms with a formal agreement to collude. Cartels are illegal in the UK, and people found guilty of cartel activity can go to prison.
The money coming into and going out of a business over a period of time. Money coming in is a cash inflow; money going out is a cash outflow.
An estimate of a business's cash inflows and outflows, month by month, for the months ahead. It shows when the business is likely to have spare cash and when it is likely to run short.

A national bank that provides financial and banking services for a country's government and commercial banks. It is responsible for managing the country's currency, money supply, and interest rates. The central bank in the UK is the Bank of England.
A Latin phrase meaning ‘all other things being equal’ or ‘all other factors held constant’.
The model showing income moving between households and firms, with injections from investment, government spending and exports, and withdrawals through saving, taxation and imports.
A measure of unemployment based on the number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits. It usually gives a lower figure than the Labour Force Survey, because not everyone seeking work claims.
An asset a borrower promises to a lender, which the lender can take and sell if the loan is not repaid.
Firms cooperating instead of competing, for example to fix prices, share out customers or limit output.
An economy where the government controls the allocation of resources and distribution of goods and services.
A bank that accepts deposits from households and firms, makes loans to them, and provides a payments system. Also known as a retail bank or high street bank.

Member countries remove tariffs and quotas on trade; Member countries adopt a common external tariff on trade with non-members; Free movement of factors of production (labour and capital) between member countries. e.g. European Union (EU)
Natural resources that are non-excludable but rivalrous, such as fish in the ocean or grazing land.
A situation in which a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country. This is based on the trade-offs between producing different goods.
The number of businesses in a market and the degree of rivalry between them. The spectrum of competition ranges from perfect competition to pure monopoly, with various market structures in between.

The main independent regulator of markets in the UK. They aim to protect competition and consumer interests in markets by investigating anti-competitive practices, reviewing mergers and enforcing consumer protection laws to ensure markets are fair.
Government and regulator action to promote competition and protect consumers, covering merger control, action against anti-competitive practices and the regulation of monopoly power.
Something that lets a business attract customers away from its rivals and earn higher profits than they do.
When a government deliberately pushes down the value of its currency to make exports cheaper and gain a trade advantage.
Setting a price at or close to rivals' prices.
A firm's ability to win sales from its rivals, on price or on quality.
Goods bought and used together, so that a fall in the price of one raises demand for the other. They have a negative cross elasticity of demand.
Goods that are used together, such as a games console and its games.
When the market fails to provide a good or service at all e.g. public goods like national defence or street lighting.
Indicators that combine several single indicators into one index to provide a more rounded view of development.
The share of total market output or revenue held by the largest firms in a market. A five-firm concentration ratio of 80% means the five largest firms account for 80% of the market.
Joining with a firm in an unrelated market.
Goods and services bought by households to satisfy wants directly, rather than to produce something else.

The main measure of the price level in the UK. It is a weighted price index that tracks the average change in the prices of a representative "basket" of goods and services bought by households. The annual percentage change in the CPI is the headline rate of inflation.
The difference between what a consumer is willing to pay (their valuation) and what they actually pay. It is a measure of consumer welfare/benefit.
Spending by households on goods and services. It is the largest component of aggregate demand.
A market in which barriers to entry and exit are low and sunk costs are minimal, so the threat of new entry keeps incumbent firms from earning supernormal profit.
The selling price of one unit minus its variable cost: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit
The shared values, attitudes and habits that shape how people in a business behave, often summed up as "the way we do things here".
A business taking account of the effects of its decisions on society and the environment, and not just on its owners, beyond what the law requires.
A method of appraising a project by valuing all its social costs and social benefits, not only the private ones, and proceeding where social benefit exceeds social cost.
Adding a percentage mark-up to the cost of making each unit to set the price.
Inflation caused by rising costs of production, which firms pass on as higher prices.
A process in which new innovations and technologies replace older ones, leading to the destruction of existing businesses and industries.
Money lent to a household or firm that has to be paid back later, usually with interest.
The process by which commercial banks make loans that create new bank deposits, thereby increasing the money supply.
A sudden, sharp fall in the amount banks are willing to lend.
The risk to a lender that a borrower does not repay what it owes.
XED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded for Good A to a change in the price of Good B.
The shared beliefs, customs and way of life of a group of people.

Member countries remove tariffs and quotas on trade; Member countries adopt a common external tariff on trade with non-members; Free movement of factors of production (labour and capital) between member countries; Member countries adopt a single currency. e.g. Eurozone
Records trade in goods and services, primary income, and secondary income.
A position in which the money leaving a country to pay for imports, income and transfers exceeds the money entering it, so the current account balance is negative.
Day-to-day spending on public sector wages, such as payments to teachers and nurses, and on the consumption of goods and services such as medicines and utilities.
Member countries remove tariffs and quotas on trade; Member countries adopt a common external tariff on trade with non-members. e.g. MERCOSUR (Southern Common Market)

Caused by a lack of aggregate demand in the economy, leading to job losses during economic downturns or recessions. For example, during the 2008 financial crisis, many businesses reduced their workforce due to falling demand for goods and services.
A deficit that occurs due to the economic cycle, typically widening during recessions and narrowing during booms, as tax revenue and government spending fluctuate with economic activity.
Making the desired option the option that is automatically selected if the consumer does not make an active choice. e.g. organ donation opt-out systems.
A sustained decrease in the general/average price level, giving a negative inflation rate.
The quantity of a good/service consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price in a given time period.
The quantity of workers that firms are willing and able to employ at a given wage rate.
Unemployment caused by too little aggregate demand. It rises in a recession, so it is also called cyclical unemployment (unit 2.5.1).
Inflation caused by aggregate demand rising faster than the economy can increase its output.
Anything about the customers in a market, such as their culture, tastes or language, that affects how much of a product they want to buy.
Policies used by the government or central bank to shift the aggregate demand (AD) curve in order to achieve macroeconomic objectives such as low inflation, low unemployment, and economic growth.
When a large firm splits into two or more separate, independent businesses.
A good that generates negative externalities, imposing costs on society beyond the private costs incurred by the producer.

The loss of value of capital goods over time due to wear and tear, obsolescence, or other factors. Depreciation reduces the productive capacity of the economy and must be accounted for when measuring net investment.
The removal of legal barriers and rules governing a market, intended to increase competition and efficiency by making entry easier.
Demand for a good or factor that arises not for its own sake but because it is needed to produce something else. Demand for labour is derived from demand for the output that labour produces.
A high-income economy, also called a mature economy, where most people work in services and growth is slow but steady.
A low-income economy where many people work in farming and literacy and life expectancy are lower.
Economic activity that runs on the internet and digital technology, such as online shopping, apps, streaming and social media.

The phenomenon where adding more of a variable input (like labour) to a fixed input (like machinery) results in smaller increases in output after each input is added. This is because the fixed input becomes a constraint, leading to inefficiencies.
Levied on income or profits, such as income tax, corporation tax, and National Insurance.
Deliberate changes in government spending and taxation to influence economic activity.
The unfair treatment of individuals based on characteristics such as gender, ethnicity, age, or disability, rather than their abilities or qualifications.
The reasons why ATC starts to increase as the size/output of a business becomes too large. These are internal to the firm and cause LRAC to rise.
A decrease in the rate of inflation. Prices are still rising, but at a slower pace.
Income available for spending after direct taxes, such as income tax, and after adding government transfer payments, such as benefits.
How a product gets from the producer to the customer, and where customers can buy it.

A form of specialisation where the production process is split into separate tasks, with each worker assigned a specific, repetitive task - this enables the worker to become highly skilled and efficient at that task.
Firms can reinvest supernormal profits into research and development, leading to innovation and improved quality products and productive efficiency over time.
A market that changes quickly, with new products, new technology and shifting tastes, such as smartphones, fashion or video games.
How simple, quick and cheap it is to set up and run a firm in a country, from registering the company and getting permits to paying tax and enforcing contracts.
The individuals, firms and governments whose decisions make up the economy.
The repeated rise and fall in economic activity, measured by real GDP, around the economy's long-term trend. It is also called the trade cycle or business cycle.
A broader concept. It includes economic growth but also considers improvements in living standards, welfare, and quality of life.
A narrower concept that is measured by increases in real GDP.
An unexpected event that suddenly changes demand or costs across the economy.
People of working age who are not seeking work, such as full-time students, early retirees, the long-term sick, and discouraged workers.
The fall in long-run average cost as a firm increases its scale of output. Internal economies come from the growth of the firm itself; external economies come from the growth of the industry.
The value of a currency against a basket of other currencies, with each weighted by how much the country trades with it. It is also called the trade-weighted exchange rate.
A measure of how responsive one variable is to a change in another, calculated as the percentage change in the first divided by the percentage change in the second.
An economy moving from developing to developed, with fast growth, expanding industry and rising incomes.
Choices swayed by marketing, impulse, or brand loyalty.
People doing paid work, whether full-time, part-time or self-employed. In UK figures, one hour of paid work a week is enough to count.
A person who spots a business opportunity, brings together the resources needed to exploit it and accepts the risk that it might fail.
An external cost or benefit that affects the natural environment, such as air, water, land or the climate.
Everyone receives an equal share of resources or opportunities. This is objective and measurable.
The price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied, so there is no tendency for price to change. It is also called the market-clearing price.
Shares in a company, each giving its owner part-ownership and a share of any profits paid out as dividends.
Everyone receives a "fair" share of resources. This is subjective and open to debate.
The domestic approach. The firm sells the same product abroad, in the same way, as it does at home.
The group of EU countries that use the euro as their currency, with interest rates set for all of them by the European Central Bank (ECB).
The amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied when price is below equilibrium, creating a shortage that puts upward pressure on price.
The amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded when price is above equilibrium, creating a surplus that puts downward pressure on price.
The price of one currency expressed in terms of another. It determines the domestic price of imports and the foreign price of exports.
The risk that a change in the exchange rate alters the value of a payment a firm has agreed to make or receive in a foreign currency.
These aim to reduce overall demand in the economy, which can reduce imports. Examples include contractionary fiscal policy and higher interest rates.
These aim to switch demand away from imports and towards domestically produced goods and services. Examples include tariffs, quotas, and devaluation of the currency.
Goods and services produced in one country and sold to buyers in another, so money flows into the exporting country.
Action taken to lengthen a product's life by lifting sales when they level off or start to fall.
The benefit of an economic activity that accrues to third parties rather than to the producer or consumer, measured as social benefit minus private benefit.
Gains that go to third parties, who do not pay for them.
The cost of an economic activity that falls on third parties rather than on the producer or consumer, measured as social cost minus private cost.
Costs that fall on a third party, someone outside the transaction, who is not compensated for them. Noise, pollution and congestion are the usual examples.

The reasons outside of the business why as size/output of all firms in an entire industry increases. They are external to the individual firm and cause the LRAC curve to shift downwards for all firms in the industry, reducing costs.
A positive or negative spillover effect that affects a third party not directly involved in the economic transaction. Also known as external costs or external benefits.
The inability of factors of production (land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship) to move freely between different uses or locations.
The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Records flows of investment, such as FDI and portfolio investment, as well as changes in foreign exchange reserves.
An organisation, such as a bank, that takes in money from savers and lends it to borrowers.
Markets where buyers and sellers can meet and engage in the trade of financial goods/services e.g. stocks, bonds and currencies.
The Bank of England committee that looks for risks to the financial system as a whole and acts to reduce them.
The banks, building societies, insurers, investment funds and markets that handle money for households, firms and the government.
When a firm charges each consumer the maximum price they are willing to pay, capturing all consumer surplus as profit e.g. auctions.
The amount by which government spending exceeds taxation revenue in a given period. This resets each year.
Managed by the government. It is the manipulation of government spending (G) and taxation (T) to meet a desired macroeconomic objective.

Costs that do not change when output changes, at least in the short run. Rent, business rates, insurance and the salaries of permanent staff are all fixed costs. They have to be paid even in a month when the business makes nothing.
Costs that do not vary with output, such as rent and salaries.
An exchange rate system where the central bank fixes the currency at a certain value, often by pegging it to another currency.
An exchange rate system determined by market forces of demand and supply for a currency, with no government intervention.
Occurs when a country does not have enough foreign currency to pay for essential imports, which can limit economic growth and development.
Money a firm invests in another country to set up, buy or expand a business it controls there, such as a factory, an office or a chain of shops.
An agreement made today to buy or sell a currency on a set future date at an exchange rate fixed now.

Growth by merging with or taking over a business later in the supply chain. This can secure outlets and capture more profit margin. For example, if a car manufacturer merges with a car dealership, it is forward integrated.

The idea that individuals may be influenced by the way information is presented to them, rather than the actual information itself. e.g. a consumer may be more likely to buy a product that is advertised as "90% fat free" rather than "10% fat".
An economy that has no government intervention in the allocation of resources or distribution of goods and services.
The problem that, because a public good is non-excludable, people can consume it without paying. Firms therefore cannot charge for it and the free market fails to provide it.
Member countries remove tariffs and quotas on trade; Each country retains its own trade policy with non-members. e.g. USMCA (the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement)

Short-term unemployment that occurs when people are between jobs, such as recent graduates or those who have voluntarily left a job to find a better one. For example, a software engineer may leave their current position to search for a role that offers better career growth or a higher salary. During this search period, they are considered frictionally unemployed.
Producing at that maximum, with no resources standing idle.
The level of real GDP at which all of the economy's resources are in use, so output cannot rise any further in the short run.
The four roles money performs: a medium of exchange, a measure of value, a store of value and a method of deferred payment.

A framework for analysing strategic decision-making, where the outcome for each participant depends on the actions of others. In oligopoly, firms must consider the potential reactions of rivals when making decisions about price, output, and marketing strategies.
Real GDP divided by the population, giving the average income per person. To compare countries, it is usually adjusted for differences in the cost of living.
The mixed approach. The firm treats the world as one market but adapts the product or marketing where local differences make it worthwhile. This is glocalisation.
The barriers that stop workers moving between areas to take up work, such as housing costs, family ties and regional differences in the cost of living.
A measure of income or wealth inequality derived from the Lorenz curve, running from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for perfect inequality.
The increasing integration and interdependence of the world's economies.
Selling a global brand, but adapting the product or its marketing to suit the tastes and customs of each local market.
When government intervention to correct a market failure results in a larger net welfare loss or a less efficient allocation of resources than before the intervention.
The government can provide merit goods directly, such as public education or healthcare. This ensures that these goods are available to all consumers, regardless of their ability to pay.
GDP is the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given year. It is the primary measure of economic activity and growth.

GDP plus net income from abroad - the income earned by a country's residents from overseas assets, minus the income earned by foreign residents from assets located domestically. (GNI is also referred to as GNP.)
Sales revenue minus cost of sales. Cost of sales is the direct cost of making or buying the goods that were sold, such as materials, stock bought in for resale and the wages of production staff.

Suggests that economic growth is directly related to the level of savings and investment in an economy. A higher savings rate allows for more investment in capital goods, which can lead to increased productivity and economic growth.

The idea that individuals may be influenced by the decisions of others, rather than making their own independent decision. e.g. buying an Xbox because all your friends have one, even though you prefer the games available on a PlayStation.
Joining with a firm in the same industry at the same stage of production, usually a competitor.
A country an MNC sets up in. Its home country is where its head office is.
A composite measure of development combining life expectancy, mean and expected years of schooling, and gross national income per head, scored between 0 and 1.
A United Nations measure that combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita) into one score between 0 and 1.
Any market that is not perfectly competitive, so firms have some power over their price. Monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly are all forms of imperfect competition.
When buyers or sellers lack the information they need to make the best decision.
A limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported in a period.
Goods and services bought from another country, so money flows out.
The flow of money a person or household receives over a period of time, such as wages, benefits, interest, rent and profit.
YED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in consumer income.
The unequal distribution of earnings, such as wages, rent, interest, and profit. Income is a flow of money over a period of time.
A figure expressing the value of a variable relative to a base year, which is set to 100. An index of 112 means the value is 12% above its base-year level.
A tax on spending, such as VAT or fuel duty, which the seller pays to the government.
A tax levied on goods and services when they are purchased, such as VAT or sugar tax. It is paid indirectly by the consumer via the producer, so affects the supply curve rather than the demand curve.
A product whose demand falls when income rises, so YED is negative.
A sustained increase in the general/average price level of goods and services in an economy.
A situation where one party lacks the information needed to make an informed decision.

The government can provide information about the benefits/costs of certain goods, such as public health campaigns about the importance of vaccinations or the health costs of smoking. This can increase/decrease the D=MPB curve, internalising the externality.
Income from outside of the closed economy that enters the circular flow of income (Government Spending, Investment, and Exports).
The process of developing an existing product, process or idea to improve it, make it more efficient, or adapt it for a new purpose by adding new features.
Inorganic growth is growth achieved through mergers or takeovers of other businesses.
A contract in which a firm pays a regular sum, the premium, and the insurer agrees to pay compensation if a specified loss happens.
Two businesses coming together under one owner, through a merger or a takeover.
Legal rights over ideas and creative work, such as patents, trademarks and copyright.

1. When countries rely on each other for trade, investment and supplies, so that what happens in one economy affects the others. 2. When each firm's sales and profit depend on what its rivals do, so it has to predict their reaction before it acts.
The cost of borrowing money, or the reward for saving it, shown as a percentage of the amount borrowed or saved per year.
The cost of borrowing and the reward for saving.
The reasons within a business why Average Total Costs fall as size/output of the business increase. These are internal to the firm and cause LRAC to fall.
Making the producer or consumer pay for the external cost, so it becomes part of their private cost and the price.
Money, goods or expertise given or lent on generous terms by one country, or by an organisation such as the World Bank, to help another.
The ability of a country's goods and services to compete successfully in global markets.
Government action to correct market failure or to change the outcome a free market would produce, through measures such as taxation, subsidies, regulation and direct provision.
These aim to increase productive capacity through government spending.
The creation of entirely new and original products, processes or ideas that have not existed before.
Spending by firms on capital goods, such as machinery, factories, and technology, in order to increase future productive capacity.

A bank that does not take deposits from the general public, but instead provides services to firms, governments and institutional investors, such as raising finance, advising on takeovers and trading securities.
Trade in services, such as banking, insurance, tourism and education.
The pattern by which a depreciation first worsens the current account, because contracts and habits fix quantities in the short run, and only improves it once demand has had time to respond.
A way of managing stock in which materials arrive just as they are needed and products are made to meet orders, so the firm holds little or no buffer stock.
Continuous improvement through many small, regular changes, most of them suggested by the workers who do the job.
The total of those in employment and those unemployed who are actively seeking work.
Output per worker, or output per hour worked, over a given period. It is the main measure of how efficiently labour is being used.
Production that uses a high proportion of labour compared with capital, so wages are a large share of costs.
The curve showing that tax revenue rises with the tax rate up to a point and falls beyond it, because very high rates discourage work, encourage avoidance and shrink the tax base.
There is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded (QD). As price rises, QD falls (ceteris paribus).
The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility
As more units are consumed, the extra utility gained from the next unit falls.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
An approach to production that aims to cut waste of every kind, such as materials, time, stock and faulty products, while keeping quality high.
Paying to use an asset, such as a vehicle or a photocopier, for a set period without buying it.

Defined by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) as a firm with a market share of 25% or more. For example, Google has a market share of over 90% in the search engine market in the UK, making it a legal monopoly.
Laws passed by Parliament that ban or require something. Since 1 June 2025 it has been illegal for shops in England to sell single-use vapes, which were being thrown away as litter in large numbers.
A central bank lending to a commercial bank that is short of cash and cannot borrow anywhere else.
The owners can lose no more than the money they have put into the business.
The ease with which an asset can be converted into cash without loss of value.
The proportion of a bank's assets that are held in liquid form, such as cash, reserves at the central bank and easily marketable securities.
The percentage of adults, aged 15 and over, who can read and write.
The pay a worker needs to cover basic needs, such as food, housing and healthcare, where they live.
A fixed sum borrowed for an agreed period and repaid in regular instalments, with interest.
A period where all factors of production are variable. Firms can build new factories, hire more workers, etc. Supply is therefore more price elastic in the long run.
The large number of niche products that each sell only a few units, but together can make up a big share of sales.
Long-run aggregate supply is the total potential output of an economy when all factors of production are fully and efficiently employed.
An increase in the economy's productive capacity. This is the maximum possible output the economy could produce if all resources were fully employed. Also known as potential growth.
A diagram plotting the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of population. The further the curve lies below the 45-degree line of perfect equality, the greater the inequality.
The goals a government sets for the performance of the whole economy.
An exchange rate system where the central bank fixes the currency within a certain range, but allows it to fluctuate within that range.
Requiring consumers to make the desired choice legally. e.g. requiring car owners to have third-party insurance.
The amount by which actual or planned sales are above the break-even point: Margin of safety = Actual output - Break-even output
change in TC/change in Q, which is the additional cost incurred when producing one more unit.
The extra output produced by one more worker.
The additional output produced by employing one more unit of a variable factor, typically labour.
change in TR/change in Q. This is the additional revenue from selling one more unit.
The extra revenue a firm gains from employing one more unit of a factor, found by multiplying its marginal physical product by marginal revenue. It is the firm's demand curve for labour.
The extra satisfaction a consumer gets from one more unit of a good.
The extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit.
A rise in an asset's price far above what its underlying value can justify, driven by buyers expecting further rises.
The point where market demand equals market supply.
When the free market, through the price mechanism, fails to allocate scarce resources efficiently, leading to a social welfare loss.
The percentage change in the size of a market over a period, measured by sales value or volume.
A diagram that plots the brands in a market against two features customers care about, such as price and quality.
A business finds out what consumers want first, then designs and produces to match.
Where a product sits in customers' minds compared with its rivals, for example cheap and basic, or expensive and high quality.
A firm's ability to influence the prices it charges customers or pays suppliers.
Collecting and analysing information about customers, competitors and the market a business sells in.

When individuals or institutions manipulate financial markets for their own benefit, often at the expense of other market participants. This can lead to market failure by distorting prices and reducing trust in the financial system.
Dividing a market into groups of customers who share similar characteristics and needs, so a firm can target one or more of them.
One firm's sales as a percentage of the total sales in its market.
These aim to increase productive capacity by removing government interventions.
Finding out what customers want and persuading them to buy the firm's product.
A depreciation improves the current account only if the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports add up to more than 1: PED_exports + PED_imports > 1
A large market where similar products are sold to most types of customer, such as toothpaste, crisps or smartphones.

A legal maximum price set below the equilibrium price, used to make essential goods and services such as food or rent more affordable for consumers. It causes a contraction in supply and an expansion in demand, leading to excess demand in the market.
Total income divided by the number of people, the ordinary average.

The middle value when data are ranked in order, so that half the values lie above it and half below. Median income is often preferred to mean income because it is not pulled upwards by a few very high earners.
The income of the person in the middle when everyone is ranked from lowest to highest income.
A good that generates positive externalities, benefiting society beyond the private benefits received by the consumer.
Targeting very small groups of customers, or individuals, with products and offers tailored to them, using data on what they search for and buy.
People moving from one place to another to live, usually to find work or higher pay.
The lowest level of output at which a firm can achieve the lowest possible average total cost in the long run.

A legal minimum price set above the equilibrium price, used to guarantee income for producers such as farmers, or to discourage consumption of demerit goods. It causes an expansion in supply and a contraction in demand, leading to excess supply in the market.
The lowest hourly pay an employer can legally give a worker.
An economy that combines elements of both free market and command economies, with varying degrees of government intervention to correct market failures.
Managed by the Bank of England, which is independent. It is the manipulation of interest rates and the money supply to meet a desired macroeconomic objective.

Member countries remove tariffs and quotas on trade; Member countries adopt a common external tariff on trade with non-members; Free movement of factors of production (labour and capital) between member countries; Member countries adopt a single currency. e.g. Eurozone
The total amount of money available in an economy at a particular point in time.

A market with many firms and low barriers to entry, where each firm sells a slightly different product. Hairdressers, cafés and takeaways in a town are typical examples. Where the spec lists "imperfect competition" alongside monopoly and oligopoly, this is the structure it means.
A market structure in which a single firm supplies the whole market. In UK competition law a firm with a market share of 25% or more is treated as having monopoly power.
The ability of a firm to set prices above the competitive level due to a lack of competition. Any firm with 25% or more market share is considered to have monopoly power.
A market with a single or dominant buyer, which can use its buying power to force down the price it pays - for example an employer that is the main purchaser of labour in a local market.
When individuals or institutions take on excessive risk because they do not bear the full consequences of their actions. In financial markets, this can lead to market failure in the following ways:
The proportion of extra income spent on domestic goods and services.
The proportion of extra income spent on imports.
The proportion of extra income saved.
The proportion of extra income paid in tax.
A business with operations, such as factories, offices or shops, in more than one country (unit 2.4.1).
The multiplier is the process by which an initial injection, such as an increase in government spending, investment, or exports, leads to a larger final increase in national income and real GDP.
The process by which an initial change in spending leads to a larger final change in real GDP.
The total amount of money that a government owes to creditors. This is the accumulation of past deficits and surpluses over time.
The total value of output, expenditure, and income generated in an economy over a period of time, usually a year.

A market in which economies of scale are so large relative to demand that one firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than two or more could. Water and rail infrastructure are examples.
The level of unemployment that exists when the economy is at full employment, consisting of frictional and structural unemployment.
A cost imposed on a third party not involved in the transaction, so social cost exceeds private cost and the market over-produces relative to the socially optimal level.
Exports minus imports (X - M), a component of aggregate demand. A surplus (X > M) adds to AD, while a deficit (X < M) subtracts from it.
When a product becomes more useful to each user as more people use it.

Non-profit organisations that operate independently of governments. They often focus on specific development issues such as education, healthcare, or human rights. NGOs can provide aid, implement development projects, and advocate for policy changes to support sustainable development.
A small, specialised part of a larger market, with customers who want something particular, such as gluten-free bread or kit for left-handed golfers.
Gross domestic product measured at current prices, with no adjustment for inflation. It rises when prices rise even if output has not changed.
A value measured in the prices of the time, with no adjustment for inflation. Figures at current prices are nominal.
Where it is impossible or extremely costly to prevent non-payers from consuming the good once it is provided.
A not-for-profit organisation, independent of government, that works on a social or environmental problem. Oxfam and Save the Children are UK examples.
Winning customers through anything other than a lower price, such as quality, branding, advertising or where the product is sold.
Finite and cannot be replenished once depleted (e.g., oil, coal, natural gas). Their use involves a high opportunity cost for future generations.
One person's consumption does not reduce the amount available for others.
Any restriction on imports other than a tariff or a quota.
A product whose demand rises when income rises, so YED is positive.
The minimum profit required to keep a firm in the industry, so TR = TC. Also known as the break-even point.
Subjective statements that express an opinion or a value judgement about what ought to be.
These aim to achieve a social, environmental, or charitable mission. Any surplus is reinvested into the cause rather than distributed as profit.

A concept in behavioural economics that refers to subtle interventions or changes in the choice architecture that influence people's behaviour in a predictable way without restricting their freedom of choice.
The barriers that stop workers moving between jobs or industries, usually because they lack the skills, qualifications or training the new occupation requires.
Moving part of a firm's production or services to another country.
A market structure dominated by a few large firms, with high barriers to entry and interdependence, so each firm must consider how rivals will react to its decisions.
Gross profit minus other operating expenses. These are the costs of running the business that are not tied to each unit sold, such as rent, office salaries, marketing and utility bills.
The value of the next best alternative foregone when making an economic decision.
Organic growth is growth generated from within the business using its own resources.
The shared values and habits that shape how people in a business behave.
An output gap is the difference between the actual level of real GDP and the potential level of real GDP, which is the level of output produced when the economy is at full capacity.
Paying another firm to carry out work the business used to do itself.
An arrangement that lets a business take its bank account below zero, up to an agreed limit.
Money the owners put into the business themselves.
When the market fails to provide a good or service in the socially optimal quantity, leading to either:
A legal right that lets an inventor take action against anyone who makes or sells their invention without permission. A UK patent lasts up to 20 years if it is renewed each year.
Launching at a low price to win market share quickly, then raising it.

The difference between two percentages, found by subtracting one from the other. A rise in interest rates from 4% to 6% is a rise of two percentage points, but a 50% increase - the two are not interchangeable.
A market structure with many buyers and sellers, an identical product, perfect information and no barriers to entry, in which firms are price takers and earn only normal profit in the long run.
A labour market where there are an infinite number of identical buyers of labour (businesses) and an infinite number of identical workers.

A persistent current account deficit can lead to a build-up of foreign debt, which may require higher taxes or spending cuts in the long term. It can also lead to a loss of confidence in the domestic currency resulting in depreciation and reduced Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows.

A persistent current account surplus can lead to inflationary pressures in the domestic economy due to increased aggregate demand. It can also lead to over-reliance on exports and vulnerability to external shocks, such as a global recession or changes in trading partners' demand.
The curve showing the short-run inverse relationship between unemployment and the rate of inflation. In the long run it is taken to be vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
A tool the government or the central bank uses to steer the economy towards its objectives (unit 2.6.1).
The international approach. The firm treats each country as a separate market, with its own products and marketing, often run by local managers.
A benefit received by a third party not involved in the transaction, so social benefit exceeds private benefit and the market under-produces relative to the socially optimal level.
Objective statements that describe'what is', 'what was', or 'what will be' in the economy.
An increase in the economy's productive capacity. This is the maximum possible output the economy could produce if all resources were fully employed.
When a low-paid worker who earns more is barely better off, because they pay more tax and lose means-tested benefits at the same time.
Setting a price below cost to force rivals out of the market, then raising it.
An organisation that campaigns to change the behaviour of businesses or governments, such as Greenpeace on the environment or Amnesty International on human rights.
A website that lists the prices of the same product from many sellers side by side, used for things such as energy, flights and broadband.

Charging different prices to different consumers for the same good, where the price difference does not reflect a difference in costs. It requires market power, the ability to separate consumers and different price elasticities of demand.
PED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price.
Measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's own price. It helps us understand how easily, quickly or cheaply producers can increase output when the price rises.
A number that shows the price level in one period compared with a base period, which is set at 100.
The way changing prices allocate scarce resources in a free market, through the rationing, incentive and signalling functions of price.
Launching a new product at a high price, then lowering it over time.
The approach a firm takes to setting the price of a product over time.
New information collected first-hand by the business, for its own purpose. It is also called field research.
Managers may pursue their own objectives, such as higher salaries, sales maximisation, or perks, instead of the owners' goal of profit maximisation.
The benefits/utility derived from consumption received by the consumers directly involved in the transaction.
The costs of production incurred by the producers directly involved in the transaction.
A good that is rival and excludable, so one person's consumption prevents another's and non-payers can be shut out. Most goods traded in markets are private goods.
Private sector organisations are owned by private individuals or shareholders. Their main objective is usually profit, and they include sole traders, partnerships, and companies.
The transfer of assets or services from the public sector to the private sector, on the argument that the profit motive raises efficiency.
A new or improved way of producing or delivering a product, such as the same bakery installing ovens that bake twice as many loaves an hour.
The difference between the price a producer is willing to accept (their cost of supply) and the price they actually receive. It is a measure of producer welfare/profit.
The time between starting work on a new product and putting it on sale.
Making a product different from rival products in ways that customers value.
A new or improved good or service, such as a bakery launching a gluten-free range.
The stages a product's sales pass through over time, from launch to withdrawal.
The process of combining various resources (inputs) and the factors of production to create goods and services (outputs).
A curve that shows the maximum potential output combinations of two goods or services an economy can achieve when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed.
A curve showing the largest combinations of two goods an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed.
Resources are used in the most efficient way possible, minimising costs of production and maximising output.
The firm is not producing at the minimum point of the AC curve, so there is higher than necessary costs.
The maximum possible output of an economy that occurs when all resources and factors of production are being utilised to their maximum. Also known as the full employment level of output.
Output per unit of input per period of time. Rising productivity means more output from the same resources, which lowers unit costs.
An organisation that sets the qualifications and standards for a profession. Accountants, for example, must pass a professional body's exams before they can call themselves chartered.
The amount by which a business's total revenue exceeds its total costs.
Operating profit minus interest paid on the firm's loans. It is also called net profit.
The objective of producing at the level of output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, so that the gap between total revenue and total cost is at its greatest.
These aim to generate financial returns for owners. Most private sector firms fall into this category.
The objective of maximising the return earned on the bank's assets for its shareholders.
A tax where the percentage of income paid in tax rises as income rises. Examples include income tax and inheritance tax.
Communicating with customers to make them aware of a product and persuade them to buy it.
Legal rights to own, use, and transfer property e.g. land, buildings, and intellectual property.

A tax where the percentage of income paid in tax remains constant regardless of income level. There are few examples of purely proportional taxes, but some flat-rate taxes can be considered proportional.
Government policies that restrict imports to shield domestic producers from foreign competition.
Setting a price for its effect on how customers see the product.
A good that is non-rival and non-excludable, so it will not be provided by the free market. National defence and street lighting are examples.

Refers to the ownership of enterprises by the government. It aims to provide essential goods and services, ensure equitable distribution, and control natural monopolies. Nationalisation is a form of public ownership where private enterprises are taken over by the government.

Public sector organisations are owned and funded by the government. Their main purpose is usually to provide a service, such as the NHS, state schools, or the BBC, and they are funded mainly through taxation.
A benefit of selling abroad that attracts a firm to expand there.
An exchange rate that equalises the cost of an identical basket of goods between two countries. It is used to compare living standards more fairly than market exchange rates allow.
A market structure where there is a single seller of a product with no close substitutes. For example, a local water company like Thames Water.
A problem in the home market that drives a firm to look for sales abroad.
Information about opinions, feelings and reasons, such as why customers prefer one brand to another. It explains behaviour but is hard to turn into numbers.
Setting standards for each stage of production and checking work against them as it is done, so faults are stopped before the product is finished.
Checking finished products, or samples of them, and rejecting any that are faulty.
Values that divide a distribution into equal-sized groups when the data are ranked in order. Quartiles divide it into four groups and deciles into ten; they are used to describe how income is spread.
Information that can be counted or measured, such as how many people would buy a product or how much they would pay. It is used to estimate demand and sales.
A monetary policy in which the central bank creates money electronically to buy financial assets, mainly government bonds, in order to raise their price, lower yields and increase lending.
The central bank creating new money electronically and using it to buy assets, mostly government bonds, to increase the money supply.
A physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported over a period. It restricts supply and so raises the domestic price.
How fast a variable is growing, as opposed to its level. Inflation falling is a fall in the rate of change of prices, not a fall in prices themselves.
The assumption that economic agents weigh up costs and benefits and choose the option that maximises their own welfare - consumers maximising utility and firms maximising profit.
Cutting capacity to match demand, for example by closing a site, selling machinery, cutting shifts or making staff redundant.
Gross domestic product adjusted for inflation, so that it measures the change in the volume of output rather than the change in prices. It is the measure used to judge economic growth.
Income adjusted for inflation, measuring the quantity of goods and services it will actually buy. Real income falls when prices rise faster than nominal income.
A value adjusted for inflation, so it shows what has happened to the amount bought or produced. Figures at constant prices are real: they are valued at the prices of one base year.
Occurs when wages are set above the market-clearing level, leading to excess supply of labour. This can be caused by minimum wage laws or trade union negotiations.
A fall in real GDP for two consecutive quarters, that is, six months of negative economic growth.
Government action that moves income or wealth from better-off households to worse-off ones, through taxes, benefits and public services.
When an employer dismisses a worker because their job is no longer needed, not because of how they did it.
A tax where the percentage of income paid in tax falls as income rises. Examples include VAT and demerit good taxes e.g. tobacco and alcohol duties.
Laws and rules implemented by the government and regulatory bodies to influence the behaviour of firms and individuals.
Regulatory capture occurs when regulated firms gain too much influence over the regulators and shape the rules in their own favour rather than in consumers' interests.
Higher export prices compared with competitors usually indicate weaker competitiveness.
When household income is below a certain proportion of median income in an economy.
Rising unit labour costs compared with competitors usually indicate weaker competitiveness.
Can be replenished over time (e.g., wind power, solar energy, forests). Their use can be sustainable.
The work a business does to discover new knowledge and turn it into new products or new ways of making them.
Limiting the number of options available to consumers to simplify decision-making and reduce choice overload. e.g. simplifying menu options in a restaurant.
Actions by a firm that limit competition, either against rivals or against the firms it trades with.
The profit an investment earns as a percentage of its cost (unit 1.1.2).

How output responds when all factors of production are increased together in the long run. Returns are increasing, constant or decreasing as output rises by more than, the same as, or less than the inputs.

1. The chance that a decision turns out worse than expected, so that a business makes a loss or fails. 2. An unknown outcome whose chances can be measured, usually from past data, so a probability can be put on it.
Relying on simple rules or past choices instead of a full calculation.
Selling as many units as possible without making a loss, so the business at least breaks even.
The money a business receives from selling its output, before any costs are taken off. It is also called total revenue or turnover.
The number of units a business sells in a period, such as a week, a month or a year.
The group of people who take part in the research, chosen to stand for the whole market. A firm cannot ask everyone, so it asks a sample and assumes the rest think the same.
Aiming for a satisfactory level of profit that keeps the owners happy, instead of the most profit possible.
A market where most people who want the product already have it, so sales grow slowly and come mainly from replacements.
When there are finite resources (e.g., land, labour, capital) but infinite human wants and needs.

Caused by fluctuations in demand for certain types of labour at different times of the year. For example, a ski instructor may be unemployed during the summer months when there is no demand for skiing lessons.
Data from which the regular within-year pattern has been removed, so that the underlying trend can be seen. Retail sales are seasonally adjusted to stop the December peak being read as growth.
When a firm charges different prices based on the quantity purchased or the version of the product, such as bulk discounts or premium versions. Also known as Purchasing Economies of Scale.
Using information that has already been collected by someone else, or for another purpose. It is also called desk research.
The objective of minimising the risk of losses from bad debts and risky investments.
When a firm or industry sets and checks its own standards of behaviour, without the law requiring it.
Money raised by selling shares in a company to investors, who become part owners.

A period where at least one factor of production is fixed (e.g., factory size, number of machines). Supply is typically more price inelastic in the short run as firms cannot instantly expand all inputs.

Short-run aggregate supply is the total planned output of goods and services in an economy at a given price level in a period where at least one factor of production is fixed, such as the capital stock or technology.
An increase in real GDP over time. It is measured by the percentage change in the actual output of goods and services. Also known as actual growth.
A curve showing an inverse relationship between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment in the short run.
Indicators that measure one aspect of development, such as the infant mortality rate, literacy rate, or access to clean water.
A trading bloc where goods, services, capital and people move freely between members, under one set of product rules.
When employers can't find enough workers with the skills they need at the going wage.
The total benefits to society of consuming a good, including both private and external benefits.
The total costs to society of producing a good, including both private and external costs.
A business that trades to tackle a social or environmental problem and reinvests most of its profit in that aim.
The output where the social cost of one more unit equals its social benefit, written MSC = MSB on a diagram. The last unit made costs society exactly what it is worth to society.
The sum of consumer and producer surplus (Triangle A + Triangle B). It represents the total welfare in the market.
The gap between what a firm produces and the most it could produce. The firm could raise output by this much without new premises or machinery.
Occurs when individuals, firms, regions, or countries concentrate on producing a specific good or service.

When investors buy assets with the expectation that their prices will rise, rather than based on the underlying value of the asset. This can lead to market bubbles, where asset prices become detached from their fundamental value, and can eventually burst, causing widespread financial instability and loss of wealth to individuals.
A market where sales, products and customer tastes change little from year to year, such as bread, toilet roll or milk.
Any person or group with an interest in a business, because its decisions affect them or their decisions affect it.
The quantity and quality of goods and services people can afford, which depends on their real income.
A financial statement that shows a firm's revenue, costs and profit over a period, usually a year. Its older name is the profit and loss account.
Resources are both allocated and utilised in the most efficient way possible at a given point in time. This requires both allocative and productive efficiency.
A long-term shift in the share of jobs and output between the sectors of an economy.

A deficit that exists even when the economy is operating at its potential output, indicating a fundamental imbalance between government spending and taxation that is not related to the economic cycle.

Caused by a mismatch between the skills of workers and the requirements of available jobs, often due to technological change or shifts in the economy. For example, the decline of coal mining and the rise of renewable energy has led to structural unemployment in certain regions.
A home loan to a borrower with a poor credit record or low income, who is more likely than most to default.
A per-unit payment from the government to producers to lower their costs of production.

Financial incentives for consumers to choose goods or services that have positive externalities, such as subsidies for public transport or renewable energy. This reduces demand for the demerit good as consumers switch to the subsidised alternatives.
A payment from government to producers that lowers their costs, shifting supply to the right so that output rises and price falls. It is used to encourage goods with positive externalities.
Goods that can be used in place of each other, such as train and coach travel.
Costs that cannot be recovered if a firm leaves the market.
Any profit above normal profit, so TR > TC.
The quantity of a good/service producers are willing and able to produce/sell at a given price in a given time period.
The quantity of workers willing and able to work at a given wage rate.
Policies that aim to increase the productive potential/capacity of the economy by shifting the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve to the right.
Development that meets the needs of the present without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, by not depleting the natural capital growth depends on.
The risk that the failure of one financial institution triggers the failure of others and a wider financial crisis.
Firms coordinating their prices or output without any formal or spoken agreement, for example by following a price leader.
A tax on imported goods, which raises their price to domestic consumers, reduces the quantity imported and raises revenue for the government.
Unemployment caused by machines or software doing work that people used to do, such as self-service checkouts replacing cashiers.
The ratio of a country's export prices to its import prices, expressed as an index. An improvement means each unit of exports buys more imports.
When a firm charges different prices to different consumer groups based on characteristics such as age, location, or income e.g. train tickets.
The whole cost of producing a given level of output, found by adding fixed and variable costs: Total costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs
Making quality the responsibility of every employee in every department, with each stage of the work treating the next as its customer.
The total output produced by a firm.
The money a firm receives from selling its product (also called sales revenue): Total revenue = Price x Quantity sold

The government can set a cap on total emissions and auction permits that firms must purchase to emit pollutants. These can then be traded on a secondary market. This increases firms costs of production, resulting in S=MPC shifting upward and internalising the external cost. It also incentivises firms to invest in cleaner technologies.
When joining a bloc moves trade from a higher-cost producer at home to a lower-cost producer in another member country.
When a supplier lets a business take goods now and pay for them later, often 30 or 60 days later.
The trade cycle is the fluctuation in real GDP over time, with periods of boom and recession.
When joining a bloc moves trade from a lower-cost producer outside the bloc to a higher-cost producer inside it.
The reduction or removal of barriers to trade, such as tariffs (taxes on imports) and quotas (limits on the quantity that can be imported).
An organisation formed by workers to protect their rights, improve pay and secure better working conditions.
Giving up some of one thing in order to have more of another.
A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between themselves, ranging from a free trade area through a customs union to a single market.
The assumption that individuals are rational decision makers who endeavour to maximise their utility.
Payments where no good or service is received in return, such as pensions, unemployment benefits, and subsidies.

Occurs when a multinational company sets the price for goods and services sold between its subsidiaries in different countries. This can be used to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions, reducing the company's overall tax liability.
A business with operations, such as factories, offices or shops, in more than one country. It is also called a multinational corporation (MNC).
The trend rate of growth is the long-term average growth rate of an economy, which is usually measured over a period of 10 years or more.
The average rate at which real GDP grows over many years, as the economy's capacity to produce rises.
An unknown outcome whose chances cannot be measured, because there is no past record to go on.

When workers are in jobs that underutilise their skills or when they want to work more hours than they currently do. For example, a qualified teacher working part-time as a barista due to a lack of teaching vacancies is underemployed.
An individual of working age who is without work, but is willing and able to work, and is actively seeking employment.
People of working age who have no job but are available for work and actively looking for it.
The number of people unemployed as a percentage of the labour force - that is, of those in work plus those unemployed and actively seeking work.
An effect of a policy that policy-makers did not aim for, often on another objective or another group.
A feature of a product or business that customers value and rivals do not offer.
The owners are personally responsible for all of the business's debts, with no limit.
The satisfaction or happiness a consumer derives from consuming goods and services.
A view about what is morally or subjectively important. These judgements underpin all normative statements.
Costs that rise and fall with output. Raw materials, packaging, the energy used by machines and delivery charges are variable costs. Make nothing and they fall to zero.
Costs that vary directly with output, such as raw materials and hourly wages.
Money that specialist investment firms put into a small, fast-growing business, taking part ownership of it in exchange.
Joining with a firm at a different stage of the same supply chain. It runs in two directions.
Marketing designed to be shared by the people who see it, so it spreads from person to person at little cost to the firm.
Trade in goods, things you can see and touch, such as cars, medicines or oil.

A promise by firms in an industry to change what they do, agreed with the government with no law forcing them. In 2016 the food industry was asked to cut sugar in foods such as cereals, yoghurts and biscuits by 20% by 2020, on a voluntary basis.
When workers with similar skills and qualifications are paid differently based on characteristics unrelated to their job performance, such as gender, ethnicity, or age.
The price of labour, paid per hour, week or year of work.
The stock of assets a person or household owns at a point in time, such as a house, savings, shares and a pension, minus any debts.
The unequal distribution of assets, such as property, shares, and savings. Wealth is a stock of monetary value at a point in time.

The loss of social welfare that arises when output is not at the socially optimal level, shown as the shaded triangle between the marginal social cost and marginal social benefit curves. Also called deadweight loss.
Income that leaves the circular flow of income and is not passed on as spending (Savings, Taxation, and Imports).
The money available for a business's day-to-day running, measured as current assets minus current liabilities. It pays for stock, staff and suppliers before customers pay.
A lack of competition or lack of profit incentive causes a firm to become organisationally slack (lazy), leading to higher ATC.
